newsitem.title: USA: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- More flattening trades unwind.
newsitem.headline: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- More flattening trades unwind.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury yield curve continued to steepen on Thursday, largely due to technical factors on further assessment of the Federal Reserve leaving rates steady earlier in week.
The two-year to 30-year spread widened to 76 basis points -- its widest since 77 basis points on March 19, six days before the Fed raised rates.
Early Thursday, the two-year note was at 6.24 percent, while the 30-year bond jumped to 7.00 percent, its highest level since closing at 7.11 percent on April 28.

Since Tuesday afternoon, the curve has steepened by about 10 basis points, partly due to a narrower-than-expected U.S. trade deficit and another low level of jobless claims and partly due to position unwindings.
"Right now, we are adjusting ourselves to the no Fed move," said a head trader at a primary dealership. "Anything further depends totally on the economic statistics. Now we are starting fresh again."

Before Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, the the market had been fairly split as to whether the Fed would raise rates. Bets were made on both sides, making it clear half the market would be wrong.
The Fed left the federal funds rate at 5.50 percent and the discount rate at 5.00 percent.

The curve steepened five basis points after the Fed's announcement, as the two-year note totally outperformed the bond on unwindings of curve-flattening trades. Those unwindings continued on Wednesday and early Thursday morning, traders said, along with curve-steepening trades.
Market players also reported STRIPS selling in bonds and hedge fund selling in intermediates.
Most of the long-end selling is said to be coming from large hedge funds, many of whom are said to have started to feel the Fed may be behind the inflation curve.
"People had time to think about where they would be and people are now questionable about a future Fed hike," said the head trader.
At the moment, traders said a rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in July has not been factored in, evidenced by heavy buying at the short end.
Bill rates, for example have fallen as much as 17 basis points since Monday, and traders said two-year notes have solid support at the 100-8/32 level.
Yet, traders do not rule out a move to flattening next week, which would be mostly a result of Treasury auctions next week.
Doug Gray, trader at Zions First National Bank, noted supply could pose a problem, especially the two-year note auction on Wednesday.
At present, the when-issued two-year note is at 6.27 percent, but Gray speculated the issue could back up to 6.30 to 6.35 percent by auction time.
